transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-11
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Jillian Park (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (CTO - Lynx), Hannah Lee (SecOps - Lynx), Daniel O'Neal (Infra Lead - Lynx)

Summary (auto): quick discovery on private VPC deployment options. Customer wants Private (VPC) deployment vs Hosted; main concerns: network topology, peering vs private endpoints, region constraints, KMS/HSM integration, audit logs, and performance/latency. Action items captured below.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jillian: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Jillian from Redwood. Uh, quick intros 

[00:08] Samir: Hi, Samir here, CTO at Lynx. Hannah and Daniel are on from security and infra. Thanks for the time.
[00:15] Hannah: Hey all.
[00:17] Daniel: Hi.
[00:18] Marco: Great, cool. So, agenda 

- we want to understand your current infra, constraints, and then sketch out Redwood private deployment options: VPC peering, PrivateLink/private endpoints, region mapping, and what the integration looks like (KMS, SSO, audit). Sound good?
[00:30] Samir: Yep. We'll try to be concise. We're evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. For any production with customer data we want private: ideally the Redwood control plane in your managed region but model serving inside our VPC or a customer-managed account.
[00:42] Jillian: Yep, understood. Quick question: do you have a preference for cross-account VPC peering or using AWS PrivateLink/Interface VPC Endpoints?
[00:50] Daniel: We generally prefer PrivateLink for isolation and to avoid full route table peering changes, but for high-throughput talk we worry about interface endpoint ENI limits and costs.
[01:04] Marco: Right, that's a common tradeoff. Peering gives us direct L3 routing and avoids a middle hop but requires route table entries and we have to coordinate CIDR ranges. PrivateLink uses interface endpoints per AZ and you pay per-hour per endpoint and data processing. For token-heavy inference workloads egress cost and per-GB processing can add up.
[01:24] Hannah: Also, from a compliance angle, PrivateLink is nice because it leaves audit trails at the endpoint and you get AWS-managed security boundary, but we need to ensure logs flow to our SIEM. Do you support pushing logs to customer S3 or Kinesis?
[01:38] Marco: Yes, for Private deployments we can forward audit logs and request traces to customer-owned S3 buckets or an event stream. We typically integrate with the customer's KMS to encrypt at rest 

- the customer owns the CMK. We also support HSM integrations for key material if required.
[01:52] Samir: On region constraints 

- Lynx has customers in EU and NA, and some data residency rules force certain workloads to stay in eu-west-1. Is it possible to have model serving restricted to a particular region and still use Redwood's control plane?
[02:06] Jillian: Short answer: yes. Our private deployment offers a control plane in Redwood's region with model-serving nodes deployed into your VPC in the region(s) you need. For strict residency, we can deploy the control plane in a regionalized private control plane option 

- that's part of our private offering. We'll share the architecture doc.
[02:20] Daniel: If we need cross-region failover, what are the options? We don't want cold-starts that add big latency.
[02:27] Marco: You can do active-active deployments across two regions with state replication for model artifacts and cached KV store warm-up. There's latency tradeoffs; typically, for low-latency inference we recommend regional clusters pinned to the traffic region and a smart routing layer that falls back if the regional cluster is unavailable.
[02:43] Hannah: About networking specifics: we use strict NACLs and limit outbound egress. Can Redwood's nodes be placed in private subnets with NAT egress via our egress firewall?
[02:53] Marco: Yes, nodes run in private subnets. For software updates and image pulls we either use a customer-provided NAT or an approved proxy. We can also mirror images into your private ECR to avoid external pulls.
[03:05] Samir: How do you handle model updates and rollout 

- do we get canaries inside our VPC?
[03:11] Marco: Absolutely. Rollouts (canary / A-B) are orchestrated by Redwood but executed inside your environment. You control traffic split and we expose tracing. If a model exhibits quality regression we can automatically route to a fallback model.
[03:24] Daniel: On peering, if we do cross-account peering, do we need to open broad ingress for the Redwood serving subnet? We're worried about blast radius.
[03:33] Marco: For peering we only need to permit the specific subnets to talk to the serving nodes and tighten SGs to port ranges used by the runtime. We can support security groups that only allow connections from your application subnets. We also support VPC endpoints with endpoint policies to restrict access.
[03:47] Hannah: Compliance: we need SOC 2 and ISO27001 certs, plus a runbook describing how logs are collected and retained. Can you provide those?
[03:55] Jillian: Yes 

- we'll send the security packet. We also support sending audit logs to customer-owned destinations, and we can provide attestations for separation of control in our private offering.
[04:05] Samir: Performance: we have a microservice doing synchronous inference at 50-120ms SLO for small prompts. Can you hit that inside our VPC?
[04:14] Marco: Likely yes, depends on model size and instance types. For small models and optimized serving we can get low single-digit token latencies. But there's variability: network hop, ENI bandwidth, and whether using PrivateLink adds hops. We should run benchmarks.
[04:30] Daniel: What's the minimal networking footprint to get started?
[04:33] Marco: Minimal footprint: one private subnet per AZ for serving nodes, one subnet for autoscaling control plane components (if customer-managed), NAT gateway or egress path, and optionally an interface endpoint for the control plane if you prefer. CIDR allocation would need to avoid overlap with your infra.
[04:49] Samir: Cost considerations 

- PrivateLink cost vs peering vs dedicated: can you give rough numbers?
[04:56] Jillian: We'll provide a cost estimate in the follow-up. Generally, peering has less per-GB cost but more operational coordination; PrivateLink is simpler but has endpoint and data processing charges. Dedicated reserved capacity affects unit cost for serving, and egress is still charged based on cloud provider rules.
[05:10] Hannah: Encryption at rest and in transit: do you terminate TLS inside our VPC or at the edge? Where are keys stored?
[05:18] Marco: TLS is end-to-end; the serving nodes will present certificates you manage if you prefer. Keys for at-rest encryption can be in your KMS (customer-managed key). For additional assurance, we support HSM-backed keys.
[05:29] Daniel: Network monitoring 

- do you emit flow logs by default? Can we integrate with our CloudWatch/Datadog?
[05:35] Marco: We can emit VPC Flow Logs to your CloudWatch or S3, and our tracing hooks can forward traces to Datadog/Zipkin via customer endpoints. We expose per-request latency and token counts to your observability stack.
[05:48] Jillian: Quick note 

- we have a sample architecture diagram for a cross-account PrivateLink + serving nodes setup. Link: https://redwood.example.com/arch/lynx-vpc-proposal.pdf (we'll attach in follow-up).
[05:59] Samir: Ok can we dive a bit deeper on PrivateLink ENI limits? We've hit ENI per-subnet limits before.
[06:06] Marco: Sure. Interface endpoints create an ENI per AZ per endpoint. For high throughput you might need multiple endpoints or larger instance types to handle concurrency. There's also an option to colocate helper nodes in your VPC that accept batched traffic and forward to the local model serving pool to reduce the number of endpoints required.
[06:24] Daniel: That helper node idea sounds promising 

- it's basically an ingress proxy that multiplexes connections?
[06:29] Marco: Exactly, it's a small fleet in your account that handles TLS termination and batching before touching the serving runtime. It's VPC-native and reduces endpoint footprint.
[06:36] Hannah: From a compliance perspective, does having helper nodes increase our burden?
[06:39] Marco: Not significantly 

- they'd be part of your account and subject to your controls. We provide hardened AMIs and deployment scripts, but you manage security updates if you prefer.
[06:48] Samir: On identity & access: can we federate to our SAML SSO and use our RBAC?
[06:53] Jillian: Yes. SSO/SAML integration for console access and API key issuance is supported. For fine-grained RBAC on routes/models we can map to your IdP groups.
[07:03] Daniel: Do you support private EKS clusters or do you run on EC2 instances?
[07:07] Marco: We support multiple deployment primitives. Most customers run on EC2/GPU instances managed by Redwood or in your account. We also support EKS setups if you prefer Kubernetes, with a Redwood operator that handles lifecycle.
[07:18] Hannah: Any certifications on the operator?
[07:20] Marco: We have hardened operator manifests and a security checklist; we'll include those in the packet.
[07:25] Samir: For the benchmark 

- what metrics do you need from us?
[07:29] Marco: We'll need sample request payloads, typical prompt lengths, concurrency targets, P95 latency targets, and a representative dataset for quality/regression checks. Also we'll need VPC details: CIDR, allowed regions, and whether cross-account peering is allowed.
[07:43] Daniel: CIDR we can provide. We have primary in us-east-1 and a secondary in eu-west-1. Cross-account peering is allowed with signed network agreements.
[07:51] Jillian: Great. We'll plan a 1-hr bench where Redwood runs a controlled load from within your VPC and shares token latency and throughput.
[07:59] Hannah: Regarding logs retention: we retain 7 years internally. Will Redwood keep any logs unless we disable that?
[08:05] Marco: In private deployments, audit logs are stored in customer-owned destinations. Redwood keeps minimal operational logs per our retention policy, but for compliance use-cases we recommend pushing all audit data to your S3 where you control retention.
[08:18] Samir: Any gotchas with egress charges if model weights are pulled from Redwood artifact store?
[08:23] Marco: If the model artifacts are pulled into your account (mirrored to your ECR/S3) then egress is lower; if Redwood imports artifacts on your behalf across accounts then standard cloud egress applies. Mirroring is recommended for big models.
[08:36] Daniel: Ok. Last question 

- timeline. If we sign for private, how long to get us running?
[08:42] Jillian: Typical onboarding for private VPC deployment is 4-8 weeks depending on compliance gating and networking approvals. Dedicated reserved capacity can be faster. We'll propose a phased pilot 

- benching + dev sandbox, then canary prod.
[08:55] Samir: Sounds reasonable. Let's recap next steps.
[09:00] Jillian: Recap: Redwood will send architecture diagram and security packet, Marco will prepare bench playbook, Lynx will share VPC CIDR and compliance questionnaire. We'll aim to schedule the bench week of 3/22.
[09:12] Hannah: We'll get the questionnaire and CIDR to you 

- expect it this week.
[09:16] Daniel: I'll pull together region preferences and network contacts.
[09:20] Marco: Great, I'll prepare the scripts and a checklist for required IAM roles and endpoint creation.
[09:27] Jillian: Ok thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the docs and a calendar invite for the benchmark.
[09:33] Samir: Thanks, appreciate it.
[09:35] END

Notes: Transcript includes some transcription artifacts and slight speaker overlaps. Links and attachments to be provided in follow-up email.
